summary.short: Amends New York civil rights, penal and election laws on images, audio and records altered by digitization (including AI). Adds civil false-light action, crimes for intimate and fabricated records, and disclosure of deceptive political media within sixty days of elections. Subpart A effective immediately; B and C on ninetieth day.
summary.long: Part MM has three subparts on images, audio and records altered by 'digitization' (software, machine learning, artificial intelligence or other computer-generated means that realistically alter a depiction). Subpart A amends Civil Rights Law §§ 50, 51, 52-b and 52-c to cover likeness, voice and digitized images, and adds § 50-h, a private false-light action against actors who disseminate digitally-altered material containing false statements; remedies include injunctions, punitive and compensatory damages and fees, with three-year or one-year limitation periods. Subpart B amends the Penal Law so digitization does not relieve criminal liability and extends intimate-image, coercion, impersonation, identity theft and sexual-performance offenses to digitized material; new § 245.20 criminalizes disseminating fabricated records intended to cause harm, subject to listed exemptions such as satire, news reporting and initial platform dissemination. Subpart C amends Election Law § 14-106(5): political communications containing digitized deceptive media distributed within sixty days of an election must carry a prescribed disclosure, with exemptions for satire, parody and news, and injunctive relief for registered voters and candidates. Subpart A takes effect immediately; Subparts B and C on the ninetieth day after enactment.

notes: The document is Part MM (Subparts A-C) of a larger bill; the bill number A8808A comes from the registry title, not the excerpt. Inserted words are capitalised and struck words bracketed, so only changed text is annotated. Effective dates differ by Subpart: Subpart A section 6 takes effect immediately, Subpart B section 16 and Subpart C section 2 on the ninetieth day after becoming law, and Part MM section 4 defers to each Subpart. 'Digitization' is defined in several parallel texts that are not identical: Civil Rights Law 52-b(11) and 50-h(1)(D) and Penal Law 10.00(23) use 'means', while 52-c(1)(b) uses 'may also mean'. Penal Law 245.15(2)(d) strikes its earlier digitization definition and substitutes 'obscene'. The amendments to Penal Law 190.78 to 190.80-a reproduce only the opening paragraphs, and 190.80-a ends with 'and:' without the remaining text.

obligations.summary: Persons, firms, campaigns, committees or organizations that knowingly distribute or publish, with intent to unduly influence an election or deceive a voter, a political communication produced by or including digitized deceptive media must disclose the use of digitization. Visual media must carry the statement 'THIS POLITICAL COMMUNICATION WAS CREATED WITH THE ASSISTANCE OF DIGITIZATION'; auditory communications must clearly speak the statement at the beginning. Exemptions cover satire or parody, news reporting, and initial dissemination by a platform or service.
